tldr: Instead of relying on rigid, cyclic gait patterns, this work learns an acyclic gait that navigates void-filled, uneven terrain simply by making a discrete choice every 40 ms: take a step or wait. By introducing a small inverse model to correct touchdown errors, the authors also successfully transferred the learned policy to a completely different model predictive controller (OCS2) without any policy retraining.
hero_caption: Basic operation and controller transfer of CADENCE. (a) Every 40 ms, it chooses to either "wait" or take "a step to a safe candidate foothold", and (b) model predictive control (MPC) swings the leg. (c) By compensating for controller-specific touchdown errors using an inverse footstep model (IFM), touchdown errors remain well within safety margins even on a different MPC (OCS2).
overview:
When controlling quadruped robots with model predictive control (MPC), most existing studies assume fixed-period gaits such as trotting (where diagonal leg pairs move together) or static walking (moving one leg at a time). However, on rough terrain scattered with holes (voids), marching to a fixed rhythm introduces a fatal flaw: whenever a leg is scheduled to step, there may be no safe foothold within reach.

To solve this, the authors propose CADENCE, a lightweight step planner with a small action space. Every 40 ms, it makes one of at most 65 discrete choices: either "step with one leg to one of 16 safe candidate footholds around it" or "wait". When trained using reinforcement learning (PPO) without any gait schedule or explicit gait rewards, the policy naturally learned an "acyclic gait." It preserves diagonal leg coordination while freely varying step lengths and contact times depending on foothold availability.

A major hurdle in practice is tracking offset: the discrepancy between the foothold commanded by the planner and the actual touchdown position executed by the MPC. Because these offset characteristics depend on MPC formulation, switching to a different controller causes the robot to miss footholds. CADENCE introduces a lightweight Inverse Footstep Model (IFM) that maps touchdown targets back to input commands based on short history logs. By refitting only the IFM using fewer than 20,000 logged steps, the planner trained on a convex MPC was directly transferred to the nonlinear MPC toolkit "OCS2" with its weights completely frozen.

In simulation benchmarks with up to 49% voids, CADENCE achieved a 72.9% success rate, significantly outperforming OCS2's standard trot (43.0%). This demonstrates a breakthrough in breaking free from fixed cyclic locomotion to achieve flexible step selection tailored to safe terrain footholds.
contributions: Formulating a lightweight footstep planner for MPC around a compact action space, picking from at most 65 discrete options (waiting or stepping to a safe candidate) every 40 ms.
Demonstrating the emergence of an acyclic gait from a reinforcement learning setup with zero gait schedules or stepping orders, preserving diagonal coordination while breaking rhythm to avoid voids.
Introducing an Inverse Footstep Model (IFM) to absorb controller-specific touchdown errors, enabling zero-shot-like transfer of the frozen policy from a convex MPC to a nonlinear MPC (OCS2).

sections.heading: Why walking to a fixed rhythm fails on void-filled terrain
sections.summary: Conventional quadruped MPC relies on fixed-period gaits, risking missteps in environments where safe footholds are sparse. CADENCE discards gait schedules, choosing footsteps discretely from safe candidates to achieve flexible acyclic gaits, and demonstrates cross-controller transferability.
sections.details:
Navigating rough terrain full of holes (voids) requires deciding dynamically which leg to move, when, where, and over how long of a swing time. However, conventional model predictive control (MPC) frameworks typically rely on cyclic gaits with fixed timing and order, such as trotting with diagonal leg pairs or static walking one leg at a time. In sparse terrain, lifting a leg on a predetermined schedule often means there is no safe foothold within reach when the foot needs to come down.

Optimizing contact timings and footholds directly inside the MPC turns the problem into a mixed-integer program, leading to a computational explosion that prevents real-time execution. On the other hand, relying on an external planner often leads to several centimeters of controller tracking error between the target position and the actual touchdown location. Near void edges, this discrepancy easily causes the robot to fall. Crucially, tracking dynamics differ across controllers, so a planner trained on one MPC will miss footholds when deployed on another.

To address this challenge, this paper introduces CADENCE, a learning-based footstep planner. Every 40 ms (1 tick), CADENCE picks an action from a compact discrete space of at most 65 choices: either "take no step (wait)" or "step to one of 16 safe candidate footholds per leg." Without any gait schedules or phase variables, a small Transformer called the Candidate Mixer evaluates the choices against each other. Furthermore, an Inverse Footstep Model (IFM) learned from historical logs corrects controller-specific touchdown errors. This enables a policy trained via PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) on a convex MPC to transfer seamlessly, with completely frozen weights, to a more complex nonlinear MPC (OCS2).

sections.heading: How does it differ from existing footstep planning methods?
sections.summary: Prior work is categorized across model-based gait design, deep RL footstep selection, and cross-controller transfer. CADENCE stands out by jointly deciding footstep location and timing without fixed gaits, and transferring to a distinct model-based controller without retraining.
sections.details:
The related work spans three main research areas.

### Gait Design in Model-Based Control
Most quadruped MPC implementations enforce fixed-period gaits externally. Approaches that free the gait from fixed schedules include kinematic heuristics or tree searches to determine contact timings online, but evaluating search branches against MPC cost functions is computationally heavy. Recent work has used reinforcement learning to output contact schedules for MPC, but these methods do not choose footstep locations directly and remain tightly coupled to a single specific MPC formulation.

### Learning-Based Gaits and Footstep Selection
End-to-end reinforcement learning methods directly output joint torques or position targets, but their vast action spaces often sacrifice the robust guarantees of model-based control. Conversely, hybrid methods typically learn parameters of cyclic gaits (such as period and duty factor) or output heuristic footstep locations. The closest predecessor to CADENCE is ContactNet, which ranks discrete foothold candidates; however, it fixes the number of stance legs and swing durations per gait type (walk or trot) and can only replan at the exact instant a foot touches down.

### Cross-Controller Domain Transfer
Adapting policies to new systems often relies on inverse dynamics models, grounded simulation, or online adaptation. Some studies correct MPC target footholds using post-hoc regression, but these are restricted to fixed gaits and single controllers. To date, transferring an acyclic footstep planner across distinct model-based controllers simply by refitting an Inverse Footstep Model (IFM) has not been demonstrated.

sections.heading: Problem formulation: Decisions on void terrain and modeling controller errors
sections.summary: As the robot moves forward, it manages up to two swinging legs every 40 ms and selects footholds from safe candidate points. The formulation uses an inverse footstep model to cancel controller tracking offsets, defining a transfer problem between two distinct MPCs.
sections.details:
### Robot and Task Setup
The task uses a Unitree Go1 robot commanded to walk forward at a target velocity across flat ground riddled with holes (voids). The planner is invoked every $\Delta t = 40$ ms (1 tick) to output stepping decisions. The planner receives no information regarding gait schedules or periods.

### Planner Decisions
At each tick, the planner either takes no step ($\varnothing$) or selects one leg $\ell$ to swing to a target foothold $\mathbf{u}^\star$ with swing duration $T \in [0.1, 0.3]$ s, represented as $(\ell, \mathbf{u}^\star, T)$. The structural constraint enforces that at most two legs may swing simultaneously. Target footholds are picked from 16 safe candidate locations arranged in a grid near the leg's hip. The planner observes only current robot states, a 1-second history buffer, and candidate locations, operating as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) without direct access to full terrain or MPC internal states.

### Closed-Loop Footstep Mapping and the IFM
When footstep command $\mathbf{u}$ and swing time $T$ are sent to controller $c$, the actual landing position $\mathbf{o}$ deviates due to controller dynamics: $\mathbf{o} = \mathbf{u} + \boldsymbol{\delta}_c(\mathbf{s}, \ell, T, \mathbf{u})$. The offset $\boldsymbol{\delta}_c$ varies across controllers. Therefore, at execution time, an Inverse Footstep Model $I^c$ pre-compensates the command as $\mathbf{u} = I^c(\zeta, \mathbf{u}^\star)$, where $\zeta$ captures recent history and swing parameters.

### Two Problems to Solve
- **Problem 1 (Learning)**: Train a planner to maximize cumulative reward on a convex MPC (Di Carlo et al.) with randomized controller parameters across resets.
- **Problem 2 (Transfer)**: Keep the planner weights frozen, deploy it onto "OCS2" (which features nonlinear MPC and a Whole-Body Controller), and refit only the IFM using fewer than 20,000 logged steps to match or exceed OCS2's standard baseline performance.

sections.heading: CADENCE architecture: Small action spaces, candidate mixers, and error correction
sections.summary: Every 40 ms, the policy picks from a discrete action space. A Transformer-based Candidate Mixer evaluates all options, including waiting, via self-attention. Training runs on a convex MPC, and transfer to a new controller requires only swapping an Inverse Footstep Model (IFM) trained on small logs.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Small Action Space
The planner's action space is exceptionally compact. It selects 1 option out of at most 65 discrete choices: one "do-nothing" option plus 16 safe candidate footholds for each of the 4 legs ($4 \times 16 = 64$). Candidate footholds are sampled uniformly from safe terrain regions around each hip (on a 1 cm grid with a 2 cm margin away from voids).

### 4.2 Network Architecture
The robot state $\mathbf{x}_g$ and 1-second history $\mathbf{h}$ (base velocities, foot positions, scheduled contacts, past landing errors) are embedded and concatenated with each candidate's features to form tokens. A learnable embedding represents the "do-nothing" action. These tokens enter the "Candidate Mixer," a small 2-layer Transformer Encoder that compares all choices via self-attention. Each token outputs a score $\alpha_i$ and swing duration $T_i$, and an action is sampled from a softmax distribution. Zero-initialization is applied to the history projection and mixer output layers so that learning begins by evaluating candidates independently before smoothly incorporating cross-candidate comparisons.

### 4.3 Inverse Footstep Model (IFM)
The training convex MPC tracks footholds relative to moving hip positions, causing touchdowns to overshoot forward as forward velocity increases (up to 3.9 cm overshoot at 0.2 m/s). In contrast, OCS2 fixes footholds in the world frame and does not exhibit this overshoot. Because these closed-loop mappings differ drastically, an MLP $\Delta_\theta$ is trained on step logs $(\zeta, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{o})$ to map desired touchdown $\mathbf{o}$ back to command $\mathbf{u}$. When moving to OCS2, one only needs to refit this IFM using fewer than 20,000 steps logged by running frozen CADENCE on OCS2.

### 4.4 Training and Deployment
Training is performed in Isaac Lab with PPO. Terrain void ratios follow a curriculum progressing up to 40%. The reward function includes only base velocity tracking, a cost per step, and a fall penalty—entirely omitting rewards for gait period, foot clearance, or body posture. For deployment on OCS2, CADENCE connects to standard nonlinear MPC and WBC in Gazebo, converting depth-camera point clouds into a grid map to extract safe candidate footholds.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Emergent acyclic gaits and superior traversability
sections.summary: In Gazebo OCS2 benchmarks, CADENCE achieved an average success rate of 85.1%, easily surpassing standard trotting (67.8%). It developed an acyclic gait lacking fixed periods or step sequences yet naturally paired diagonal legs, while ablation studies confirmed the critical role of the IFM.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on OCS2 in Gazebo across six conditions: three void densities (26%, 38%, 49% using 12.5 cm tiles) and two commanded speeds (0.10 m/s and 0.20 m/s). Each condition ran for 100 trials (600 trials total). A trial was deemed successful if the robot crossed at least half the course without falling. Baselines included OCS2 standard trot (0.6 s period), OCS2 static walk (1.2 s period), and CADENCE ablation variants.

### 5.2 Benchmark Results
- **Traversal Success Rate**: Across five random seeds, CADENCE averaged an 85.1% success rate, outperforming OCS2-Trot (67.8%) by 17.3 percentage points and OCS2-Single (65.5%) by 19.6 percentage points. Under the harshest condition (49% voids at 0.20 m/s), where trotting fell to 40% and static walking to 35%, CADENCE maintained a 70% success rate.
- **Generalization to Unseen Terrains**: In sweep experiments extending beyond the 40% training curriculum limit (50–70% voids, speeds up to 0.25 m/s), CADENCE consistently outperformed trot, recording a 50% success rate on 70% void terrain where trot managed only 12%.

### Analysis of Emergent Gaits
CADENCE exhibited no fixed gait period or stepping sequence. Its coefficient of variation (CV) for lift-off intervals was 0.61—far higher than trot's 0.02—showing high adaptability in stepping frequency across speeds. Unconventional steps were observed, such as lifting the same leg twice in succession (accounting for 6.1% of steps). Remarkably, 98% of overlapping swing phases involved diagonal leg pairs, with a median lift-off difference of just 42 ms (about 1 tick). The policy autonomously discovered an acyclic gait that preserves diagonal coordination while freely adjusting rhythms and sequences to avoid stepping into voids.

### Ablations and the Impact of IFM
- **Leg Constraints**: Restricting the policy to move only one leg at a time (CADENCE-Single) caused the success rate to plummet to 39.6%, proving that allowing two concurrent swinging legs is essential.
- **Necessity of IFM**: Passing targets directly without an IFM (CADENCE-without-IFM) yielded only a 17.1% success rate, and using the convex MPC's IFM on OCS2 dropped it to 5.5%. A constant offset correction partially recovered performance (60.0%), but remained far behind the refitted IFM (85.1%). On flat ground, the IFM cut the root-mean-square (RMS) touchdown error from ~6 cm down to ~2 cm, matching the safety margin.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: Combining a compact action space with an inverse footstep model enables flexible acyclic locomotion on model-based controllers. Future work aims to support more controllers and expand to 3D terrains like stairs and slopes.
sections.details:
This paper introduced CADENCE, a learned footstep planner for model-based controllers. Operating on a small action space of at most 65 choices every 40 ms, it developed an acyclic gait that preserves diagonal coordination without any prescribed gait schedules or explicit gait reward terms.

By incorporating an Inverse Footstep Model (IFM) to absorb controller tracking errors, the planner trained on a convex MPC was successfully transferred with frozen weights to a nonlinear MPC (OCS2), dramatically outperforming standard gaits on void-filled terrain.

Future research directions include deploying across a wider variety of MPC formulations, reducing the number of logged steps required to refit the IFM, and validating online adaptation in the real world. Extending foothold candidate generation from flat void terrains to fully 3D structures such as stairs and slopes is also planned.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details, candidate sampling, and IFM analysis
sections.summary: Details cover deterministic annealing for efficient candidate placement, theoretical conditions for IFM error cancellation, and PPO training hyperparameters.
sections.details:
### Foothold Candidate Sampling
Instead of uniform random selection, candidates are sampled to efficiently cover safe regions:
- **Reference Candidate**: Fixes one candidate to the safe cell closest to the nominal foothold $\mathbf{q}_{\text{nom}}$ (predictive horizon $T_{\text{nom}} = 0.29$ s) that centers a symmetric stance based on commanded velocity.
- **Farthest-Point Sampling**: Selects remaining candidates iteratively by picking safe cells farthest from already selected candidates, distributing them along the region boundary.
- **Deterministic Annealing**: Applies a 4-step soft $k$-means procedure that lowers temperature to pull candidates inward while minimizing clustering energy.

### Theoretical Properties of the IFM
Because the IFM does not observe the full internal state $\mathbf{s}$, it can only cancel the mean error predictable from observation $\zeta$. The paper proves that post-hoc regression on the IFM optimally cancels touchdown errors under assumptions of landing law consistency, absence of unmodeled residuals, and command-to-landing invertibility. Although real controllers do not satisfy these assumptions perfectly, empirical results confirm that this approximation provides sufficient accuracy in practice.

### Training Hyperparameters
PPO was executed across 1024 parallel environments in Isaac Lab with a rollout length of 100 ticks, a learning rate of $3 \times 10^{-4}$, and a discount factor $\gamma = 0.99$. To ensure robustness, controller tracking weights, target clearance heights, and touchdown noise were randomized at the start of every episode.

takeaways: Letting gaits emerge from choices between footholds and waiting is far more effective on void-filled terrain than fixing a gait pattern before looking for footholds.
Restricting tick-by-tick decisions to "wait" or "step to a safe candidate" keeps the action space small while providing complete flexibility over contact timing.
Controller-specific footstep landing errors can be corrected effectively with a lightweight, post-hoc inverse model (IFM), eliminating the need to retrain the core planner.
limitations: Validation is limited to simulation environments (Isaac Lab and Gazebo), and physical robot experiments have not yet been conducted.
Refitting the Inverse Footstep Model (IFM) requires roughly 20,000 steps of logged data on the target controller, meaning it is not an entirely data-free zero-shot transfer.
Foothold candidate sampling currently assumes 2.5D flat terrain with voids, without direct support for 3D elevation changes like stairs or steep slopes.
